landscape: Human rights data fall into three families. The first measures state respect for physical integrity and civil rights. It includes standards-based annual scores coded from State Department and Amnesty International reports (CIRIGHTS, successor to CIRI, and the Political Terror Scale) and latent-variable estimates that combine many sources and model changing reporting standards (Fariss). Expert surveys (HRMI) and specialised data on torture, sexual violence in conflict and slavery (ITT, SVAC, CSAC) belong here too. Around them sit data on how states and others respond to abuses: treaty ratification and reservations, national human rights institutions, naming and shaming by NGOs and the UN, and transitional justice (TJET and related datasets).

The second family records contention. It covers protest event data (SCAD, Mass Mobilization, MMAD, Urban Social Disorder, the Crowd Counting Consortium, PolDem and national projects), nonviolent and violent campaigns (NAVCO 1-3, ARC, WiRe), revolutions (Revolutionary Episodes, RAQED, Major Episodes of Contention) and strikes. The third covers newer forms of repression and their targets. Its data include civic-space ratings (CIVICUS), digital repression and internet shutdowns (Digital Society Project, Access Now), transnational repression, restrictions on NGOs, attacks on journalists and defenders, police killings and human trafficking.

The domain has 96 HR rows. Many specialised datasets were produced for single projects and are now frozen; the core score series (CIRIGHTS, PTS, Fariss) and several protest trackers are updated regularly. Most sources rely on reports or news coverage, so changes in reporting intensity are a recurring threat to validity.

core.text: The Political Terror Scale scores the level of state terror in about 200 countries and territories each year from 1976 to 2025 on a 1-5 scale. Separate scores are coded from Amnesty International, U.S. State Department and (for recent years) Human Rights Watch reports. It is a long-running and widely used physical-integrity measure. A single ordinal score cannot separate types of abuse, and like all report-based measures it is exposed to changes in report scope and standards.

CIRIGHTS, the successor to the CIRI Human Rights Dataset, codes government respect for more than twenty rights for all countries from 1981, mainly from State Department reports. The coded rights include physical integrity, civil liberties, and workers' and women's rights, and the data add an overall human rights score. It extends the CIRI series (1981-2011), which many studies still cite. Coverage end years differ across sources (2022 or 2023), and the coding inherits the scope of the State Department reports.

The Fariss latent human rights protection scores (version 4) estimate respect for physical integrity rights for all states from 1946 to 2021. They use a Bayesian measurement model that combines standards-based scores and event-based data and lets the standard of accountability in reports change over time. They provide uncertainty estimates and longer coverage than any single source. The changing-standards assumption has been disputed (Cingranelli and Filippov 2018), and post-2011 estimates rest on fewer inputs.

NAVCO 2.1 codes the characteristics and outcomes of nonviolent and violent maximalist campaigns at the campaign-year level from 1945 to 2013, including participation, methods, regime responses and success. With NAVCO 1 (campaign list) and NAVCO 3.0 (events) it underpins research on the effectiveness of civil resistance. Only maximalist campaigns are included, and the source for violent campaigns changed between versions.

The Mass Mobilization Project records protests against governments with at least 50 participants in 162 countries from 1990 to March 2020, including demands and state responses such as arrests and killings. It is widely used for global analyses of protest and state response. Coverage depends on a limited set of newspapers, the manual lags the data, and pro-government protests are excluded by design.

choosing: For trends in physical integrity, compare a standards-based score (PTS or CIRIGHTS) with the Fariss latent scores, since the two diverge where reporting standards changed. Use HRMI for rights not covered by report-based sources and for recent years.

For protest, pick the dataset whose geographic scope and inclusion threshold match the question: SCAD for Africa and Latin America, Mass Mobilization for global anti-government protest, MMAD for autocracies, national trackers for single countries. Check news-coverage bias before comparing countries or periods.
gaps: No cross-national dataset on political prisoners or enforced disappearances exists beyond indicators inside CIRIGHTS and HRMI.
Most cross-national protest datasets stop between 2017 and 2020 (SCAD, Mass Mobilization); recent years are covered mainly by ACLED and national trackers.
Data on digital and transnational repression, NGO restrictions and attacks on defenders are new, produced largely by advocacy organizations, and have short time series with limited documentation.
